evidence: Hor. S. 1.5.104: Brundisium longae fīnis chartaeque viaeque est
terms.comment: Masculine in classical prose, feminine mostly in poetry (Lewis & Short). The plural fīnēs means borders, territory.

terms.gloss: end, outcome (of an event or a story)
evidence: Liv. praef. 10: foedum inceptū foedum exitū
Cic. Clu. 7: fīnis aliquis atque exitus (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: last, at the end (agreeing with its noun)
evidence: Sen. Ep. 16.9: via euntī aliquid extrēmum est
terms.comment: Latin often says “the end of” with an adjective that agrees: extrēmā pāgellā, on the last page, at the end of the letter (Cic. Fam. 2.13.3).

phrases.latin: Brundisium longae fīnis chartaeque viaeque est
phrases.english: Brundisium is the end of a long story and a long road
and the end of eating was the start of talking

phrases.latin: via euntī aliquid extrēmum est: error immēnsus est
phrases.english: a road has an end for the traveller; wandering has none

sources: Lewis & Short: finis · Lewis & Short: exitus · Lewis & Short: extremus
